issues.legal_issue: A tenant who timely remits the arrears demanded after receiving a rent-demand notice has not neglected to pay merely because the landlord does not receive or accept the remittance within that period.
material_facts: The rent was payable monthly, and the landlord served a written notice demanding arrears.
The tenants sent a money order within the month after receiving the notice, and it covered the arrears stated in the notice.
The landlord refused the money order.
The appellate court found no neglect to pay, but the High Court reversed that finding and ordered eviction for rent default.
issues.conclusion: The tenants had not neglected to pay. Neither statutory route to eviction for non-payment applied, and the appellate court’s decision was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(1), 12(2), and 12(3)(a) and (b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, eviction for rent default depends on neglect to pay, not on the landlord’s actual receipt of payment. A money order or demand draft sent within the specified period means the tenant has not neglected to pay. The Court applied the statutory distinction between the mandatory eviction route for qualifying arrears accompanied by neglect under Section 12(3)(a), and the conditional protection under Section 12(3)(b) in other cases.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_case and written_demand_notice_received and tenant_sent_remittance_within_grace_period and remittance_covered_notified_arrears

predicates.rent_default_eviction_case: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.written_demand_notice_received: The tenant received a written demand for rent arrears.
predicates.tenant_sent_remittance_within_grace_peri: The tenant sent a remittance within the period allowed after receiving the demand.
predicates.remittance_covered_notified_arrears: The remittance covered the arrears specified in the demand.

issues.definition: When a rent-default eviction case follows a written demand and the tenant timely sends a remittance covering the demanded arrears, the tenant is not evicted for rent default.

issues.legal_issue: Supervisory review of a final rent-appellate decision does not permit the High Court to reappraise ordinary issues as if hearing an appeal absent grave dereliction or flagrant abuse of fundamental principles of law or justice.
material_facts: The rent-control legislation provided no second appeal or revision to the High Court and intended the appellate authority’s decision to be final.
The High Court, exercising supervisory jurisdiction, reconsidered the issues decided below and substituted its findings for those of the appellate court.
The High Court acted as an appellate court rather than identifying grave dereliction or flagrant abuse requiring intervention.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in intervening under its supervisory jurisdiction; its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, the High Court has no unlimited power to correct every hardship or wrong decision. Its intervention must be confined to grave dereliction of duty or flagrant abuse of fundamental principles of law or justice where grave injustice would otherwise result. The Court also relied on the legislative intent to give finality to the rent appellate authority’s decision where no second appeal or revision is provided.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_rent_appellate_dec: The High Court reviews a final decision of an appellate authority in a landlord-tenant proceeding through supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.ordinary_reappraisal_of_decided_issues: The High Court reconsiders issues already decided as though hearing an appeal.
predicates.grave_dereliction_or_flagrant_abuse: The decision under review involves grave dereliction of duty or flagrant abuse of fundamental principles of law or justice requiring intervention to prevent grave injustice.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns a final rent-appellate decision and the High Court merely reappraises decided issues without grave dereliction or flagrant abuse, supervisory interference is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: A reasonable increase in rent may be directed as a fair and just consequential order when the rent has remained unchanged for a long time.
material_facts: The tenants had been paying the same monthly rent since 1980.
After hearing counsel, the Court considered it fair and just to increase the rent.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the tenants to pay increased rent.
issues.legal_principle: The Court made a consequential direction on grounds of fairness and justice after hearing counsel; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this direction.

predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a landlord-tenant rent dispute.
predicates.rent_unchanged_for_long_time: The tenant has paid the same rent for a long time.

issues.definition: In a landlord-tenant rent appeal, when rent has remained unchanged for a long time, a reasonable rent increase is directed.
